headline: Bass crash the Execution Rocks rip as Sound water hits prime 67 degrees
subhead: Outgoing tides firing stripers on bunker chunks while fluke action heats up in the bays.
body_markdown:
The Western Sound finally hit that magic number this week — 67 degrees — and the bass responded like they've been waiting all season for this moment. I've been watching the temperature creep up from the mid-60s, and when it crossed into the upper 60s, everything changed. The fish know it, the bait knows it, and if you've been paying attention to the signs, you know it too.

Execution Rocks has been the star of the show. The outgoing tide around the light structure has been producing keeper bass in the 28 to 34-inch range, with most fish hitting fresh bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs. The key is positioning yourself on the up-current side of the rocks and letting your bait sweep down into the white water where the current breaks. I'm using 6/0 circle hooks on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders, and the fish are taking the bait deep on the drift. The bite window is narrow — about an hour after the tide turns — but when it's on, it's on.

The Stepping Stones area has been equally productive, especially for boats working the deeper water between the light and Hart Island. The bass are staging in 35 to 45 feet, and they're responding to both live bunker and fresh chunks. What's interesting is the size of the bait they're eating — these aren't the tiny peanuts we sometimes see in June. The bunker are adult-sized, which tells me the bass are feeding aggressively and the food chain is stacked up properly.

Matinecock Point has been the sleeper spot this week. The rocky bottom off the point holds bass on both tides, but the incoming has been more consistent. I'm seeing fish in the slot range hitting bucktails tipped with pork rind or Gulp, worked slowly along the bottom in 25 to 30 feet. The white and chartreuse combinations have been most effective, especially when the water has that slight green tint that comes with the warmer temperatures.

Fluke fishing has picked up dramatically in the back bays. Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay are both producing keeper flatfish, with the best action coming on the outgoing tide when the current concentrates bait along the channel edges. The pattern is classic June fluke fishing — 3/4-ounce bucktails in white or chartreuse, tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in pearl or nuclear chicken. The key is working the drop-offs where the channels meet the flats, usually in 15 to 25 feet of water.

What's driving this action is the thermal structure that's finally locked in place. The Sound is running 67 to 68 degrees, which is that sweet spot where bass become aggressive feeders and baitfish concentrate in predictable patterns. The southwest winds we've had this week have pushed warmer bay water out into the main stem, creating temperature breaks that hold both bait and predators.

The moon phase is working in our favor too. We're coming off the new moon, which means the tides are still running strong but not so extreme that they blow out the bite windows. The current is moving bait without creating washing-machine conditions that shut down feeding.

Porgies have been thick around any structure in 30 to 50 feet, and they're running good size — plenty of keeper fish in the half-pound range. High-low rigs with small hooks and clam or squid strips are all you need. The Throgs Neck Bridge pilings have been particularly productive on the slack tides.

Looking ahead, the water temperature should continue to climb into the low 70s, which will only improve the bass fishing. The full moon is still a week away, so we'll have good current without the extreme tides that can make fishing difficult. I'm watching for the first real bunker schools to show up in force — when that happens, the fishing will go from good to spectacular. The signs are all there: water temperature, bait presence, and fish behavior all point to the season hitting its stride. Get out there while the conditions are prime.
